speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief but I want to go on record as saying I intend to support my party and oppose this bill. Had the bill been split it could have been passed two years ago and this legislation would not now be before us.
It seems to me that in some of the speeches there has been a tendency to malign the police forces of this country. Some wild charges have been made about what the police will do with wiretaps-that they will use illegal wiretaps and engage in nefarious schemes, skullduggery, and other things that are objectionable. I disagree with such accusations, Mr. Speaker. I have probably had no more than the average number of encounters with the Ontario Provincial Police who service a number of municipalities in my riding. I may get the odd speeding ticket, and that is the sum of my encounters with them. Much the same applies to the RCMP. We see the RCMP on ceremonial occasions and know of some of the work they do. I have a personal relationship with a senior officer of the force who grew up next door to me. He is a sterling character; I know his family, and hope some of the accusations levelled against the RCMP will be cleared up during the forthcoming inquiry.
I resent some of the things some hon. members have said about our police forces. Let me say that in the small area I represent our police forces are not villains. They are the protectors of our people. I sat four years on the board of police commissioners of the city of Belleville and I can tell you that Chief Doug Crosbie heads one of the finest police forces in all Canada. I am not ashamed to say I had a hand in hiring him, but I do not single him out particularly, because chiefs before him were also good. Let me also mention Carl Beattie, chief of the police force in Deseronto. When they have a barbeque at the Lion's Club, or when there is work to do at the arena, to get ready for the kids on Saturday morning, Carl is one of the boys; but everyone in the village knows that on Saturday night, when Carl Beattie is on duty, you had better not drive down the main street of Deseronto faster than you should, or carry a mickey in your hip pocket, because Carl will put you in the clink as quick as a wink.
The same is true of Charlie Fletcher in Picton. I have an Indian reserve in my riding, one of the few with its own police force. When there is a problem in Shannonville, or on the Tyendwaga reserve, Tom Maracle comes up and talks to the people. If it is an Indian problem he straightens it out.
Those kind of people protect people in my part of the country. Mr. Speaker, I submit many hon. members who have spoken recently, barring the hon. member who spoke before me and dealt with a specific part of the bill, have come dangerously close to imputing serious crimes to police forces in Canada. I object. In my opinion these small police forces will not engage in undue wiretapping. I guarantee it. Small communities never have enough money for equipment and men. They do not have enough men for wiretapping, or for the sort of wiretapping they might like to do. The municipal police budgets are never large enough to enable the police forces to do the job they want to do. Those forces are equipped with the best equipment it is possible to obtain for them in the circumstances. They try to buy equipment as good as they can afford, and keep their training methods up to date. But they make a

July 18, 1977

major decision when they decide to upgrade their radios or buy a new radar unit.
Personally I am not worried about wiretaps. Like most members of parliament 1 probably spend more time on the telephone than the average Canadian. Perhaps I use the telephone more than some other members do. If any people want to listen to my telephone conversations, they are welcome to try. Go ahead. I have nothing to hide. I am not the least bit worried about somebody tapping my telephone. I merely want the record to show that there is support in this House-I know I speak for many members-for those forces which protect Canadians. Our police forces are not a bunch of villains.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise under your chairmanship; this is the first time I have had this opportunity. I have something to add although I have spoken this afternoon on the amendment of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) about wiretapping. Everybody will realize that this legislation which is over 80-pages long, despite all the points dealt with, as I said this afternoon, is an omnibus bill dealing with the Customs Tariff, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act, wiretapping, gun control, etc. We find that the gun control section covers 44 pages of the bill, and that is why I said this afternoon that this was the most important question in the legislation, and that it would have been absolutely necessary to have a bill dealing specifically with gun control. What sort of a control? To what extent?
We are in favour of some control, and we have already had controls since World War II on ordinary and automatic weapons, but mainly since the sixties; and I should add that controls on automatic weapons are a lot stricter now, because I remember that when I had one day to have my revolver registered, I realized that the laws had become a lot more severe. We do not object to that, but we are saying that this legislation goes too far or is not precise enough, so that it frightens almost everybody. That is why I should like to convey to the House the reaction of the people in my constituency of Roberval who see in this bill not only a protection for law abiding citizens, as the minister claimed, but also in my opinion a legislation which favours the criminal to the detriment of the honest citizen. I am thinking about the farmers, the sportsmen and the businessmen of my constituency. Mr. Speaker, when 1 spoke on Bill C-83, I even proposed not only to grant permits but free permits. With all the money involved in this bill, it is simply another Loto Canada set up by the federal government and permits should be granted to those who require them, such as all farmers.
The bill specifies Indians and Inuits. I agree, but there are also other groups. I cannot imagine a farmer unable to have a permit for one or two guns, or sportsmen, and I added also businessmen. Nowadays, Mr. Speaker, if someone really wants protection, he must in a way look after himself. There is the civil defence, protection in general, of course, but I think it is
Criminal Code
essential that responsible citizens have the right to protect themselves. If a businessman does not have the right to keep a gun in his home to protect himself against bandits, that is terrible. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the situation if every bank manager, every bank teller could be armed? There would no longer be any bank robbers or at least far fewer of them would dare go into a bank with five, ten or 20 tellers. Then, they would start to be scared. But if there is a law that in fact disarms all those people, all the honest people, that forces them to hand over their weapons, who will then be favoured? Mr. Speaker, this bill will not disarm a single bandit. They will continue to keep their guns, and all the equipment they use to commit their crimes. In some stores, some banks, when robbers come face to face with a weapon, they do not show up a second time.
According to police reports, the law is not strong enough for us to abolish capital punishment. We started with doing just that; and now, we are asked to disarm all the honest people, under the pretext that crime will thereby be reduced. It is impossible to do so by proceeding in this way. The minister says he heard witness after witness. Yes, indeed, there were many in committee. I shall take a couple at random, for instance, from the report of the Canadian Police Association, and another, which I have here, from the report signed by Mr. McCann, advisor to the government or even from the report on arms control; those people are not extremists. They do not deny the government the right to exercise some control. I quote from that brief:
As responsible owners, we feel that arms control should endeavour to prevent criminals and the mentally ill from owning such weapons while responsible citizens should be allowed to enjoy their favorite sport without undue restrictions.
I consider it undue restriction to have all those people.
In the first place, the department is going to set up a committee to enact regulations, to impose taxes because people are more concerned over regulations than the act itself. And following that bill, which already contains 44 pages on firearms alone, I anticipate another volume on regulations they want to impose on each and everyone. And you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the bill emphasizes the punitive rather than the educational aspect. And that is the kind of avenue the government always follows. For instance, if a farmer forgot to register an old gun handed down from one generation to another, the officials will have the right to seize it because he did not report it.
We know how those things happen because there are confiscations every day in our area even with the present regulations because some hunter kills game that he is not allowed to kill, his gun or his rifle is confiscated or he is quietly on his way home after six o'clock and was unfortunate enough to leave his gun on the back seat, the gun is seized, a $200 to $250 gun that he will never see again. He is given a fine, and his rifle is taken away. People come to my office asking: Is it possible to get at least our rifle back after paying the fine? No. What do they do with it? We do not know, and nobody can tell us. But I think that thousands and thousands of rifles are being trafficked, I believe, by some public servants who take a wicked
80020-27*72

July 18, 1977
Criminal Code
pleasure in seizing every time they can the rifles and guns of people who need them.
I am afraid that this bill which is excessively permissive will further strip honest people of a firearm to which they are attached, a firearm they want and would then have the right to keep in their possession in their homes. That is why, as I said this afternoon, I repeat that bills like this should be selected and graded so we would have time to discuss and vote with the necessary amendments to strengthen that bill, and when it would come back to the House, I think it would be easier to pass. What did happen? It was buried in an omnibus bill and the witnesses were indeed listened to but without giving it more attention to bring in the amendments they were proposing about firearms. That is why I say that we cannot support Bill C-51, not because it is entirely bad, no, but because it is an omnibus bill and we cannot afford to get everyone into the same boat.
For example, is the registration of firearms going to cost $10 or $15? We do not know. The regulations will determine that and the regulations are not written by members of parliament but will again be written by public servants who will determine the amount of money they need to pay to have the right to own a firearm. But will those permits be renewable every year now? Every five years? Every ten years? That is another thing, we do not know yet, Mr. Speaker. 1 think there are many obscure issues in this bill and it is impossible at present for us to give our support to that part of the bill. I say that this bill operates to the detriment of honest citizens. We also find the following statements in the A. McCann report which I realize has been tabled in committee. I quote:
Estimates to the effect that 7 to 10 millions firearms are owned by Canadian citizens certainly prove that a lot of people 2 to 3 millions perhaps are interested enough in firearms to buy and maintain them. Only a few of these weapons are meant for illegal use. Although firearms owners are entirely in favour of effective controls, it seems unreasonable to subject a great number of citizens to such impracticable regulations. As for revolvers, controls on this type of firearms have existed in Canada since before the Second World War. These controls have been tightened in the sixties and since then their possession has become so difficult that it borders on prohibition.
And on that point they are right for I have made the experience myself. In spite of that, these controls did not result in a decrease of gun usage for criminal activities.
This is what I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker. Even with all those precautions, another report says that the crime rate has increased and that criminals are more active than ever. It is not by refusing everyone a permit that we can decrease the incidence of criminal acts.
A comparison of the crime rates in countries with strict gun control has proven its use, unless other appropriate factors be considered as well. For every country, the comparisons emphasize the importance of history, population, family life and mutual respect. In the case of criminals, there is a premeditated intent to violate the law. If this includes the use of a firearm, violation of another law by the criminal is therefore completely unimportant. The criminal will always be able to obtain the weapons he needs from illegal sources. This is why we cannot believe that any control or prohibition can have a concrete effect on the criminal use of firearms.
The next paragraph talks about mental patients. I believe mostly in some control at the level of weapon sales, but this control that we shall have will be another federal tax on illegal
[Mr. Gauthier (Roberval).l
sales. Instead of using the police for imposing a legal control, the government wants another licence traffic. And everyone knows what this traffic is like in politics. Everyone knows that this is the source of the whole problem. There will again be people who will not be entitled to hold permits but who will still get them because of political patronage. This will again come into play. If there was a legal commission to issue permits without any fee involved, there would be much less political influence. And this is always what I fear in such cases.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the federal government requires a permit for firearms trading, this is quite well for the trade. However, we do not want some regulations to deprive once again some honest citizens. This is what we fear in our areas especially according to the reports which I received at my office. All those who came to my office are afraid, but I think their fears will soon be justified if this goes on, because the minister mentioned that only the Indians, the Inuit and those who earn their living by hunting would have free permits, but they are not alone.
There are other Canadians who do not hunt for a living but who like that sport and who also have the right to own a gun either for their own pleasure or for their personal needs, such as farmers, tradesmen, businessmen and those who have great financial responsibilities. Mr. Speaker, 1 understand that this bill, regardless of what we might say, is going to be passed anyway, but I simply wanted explain why I was opposed to it, once again not because the whole bill is bad, but because of that famous omnibus bill that I have never swallowed and will never swallow.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF POLICY STATEMENTS ON CATTLE INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
AGRICULTURE-PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF POLICY STATEMENTS ON CATTLE INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion for this adjournment debate arose as far back as last February 4, as reported at page 2720 of Hansard.
(Mr. Lessard.]
July 18, 1977

One of the most serious criticisms of our parliamentary procedure I have noticed in close to five years spent in this House relates to a practice which is slowly but surely increasing, to the great detriment of our parliamentary tradition. I refer to the government's deliberate policy-making by order in council, or by direct ministerial authority.
This portion of the adjournment debate will deal with that situation, especially with respect to three policy announcements which were made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) during the last Christmas recess, dealing with Canada's beef cattle industry, at a time when no proper debate or comment in the House was possible. Today, seven months later, as we prepare to adjourn for a summer recess, we find there has been no opportunity to examine and debate these policy pronouncements, especially in committee.
The first one was on December 23, 1976, which was the announcement of Canada's offshore beef quotas, against Australia, New Zealand, and United States beef imports into Canada. The facts which should have been pointed out in a proper debate in committee, immediately after our Christmas recess, would include this long overdue action which was a full year late. Cattlemen had asked for action more than a year earlier. Approximately nine months before this announcement the signs were clearly evident that we were headed for massive levels of offshore beef imports over the remainder of 1976, a 60 per cent increase in the offshore beef imports over 1975 which came to a total of 186 million pounds. This is the equivalent of approximately 535,000 Canadian cows. These came in at very badly discounted prices of as much as 31 cents per pound below the equivalent beef entering the United States from offshore. During 1976 there was the largest supply of domestic beef in Canada's history. The result was a massive displacement of our fresh cow beef to the United States market.
I want to point out that I have no criticism of Canada's participation in the North American market, but those displaced cows moved to that market because our own market was $3 lower due to offshore imports. That exercise cost our Canadian cow market at least $30 million. The most sinister aspect of this 1976 situation was that it was so deliberate that no action was taken until a year later when the damage was done. Beef to the consumer was held at cheap levels, and the control policy and the cost of living factor appeared to be working for the consumer's benefit.
The second announcement occurred on January 4, 1977. The minister announced his cow-calf stabilization policy for the calendar year 1977, following the minister's own stabilization policy. 1 have no quarrel with that aspect, but I do quarrel with the fact that this cow-calf policy was not retroactive to 1976. That was the worst year ever in our cattle industry with costs of production taken into account.
The minister had repeatedly promised this policy would be announced in 1976 for 1976, including a promise to the provincial ministers of agriculture during the summer or fall of
Adjournment Debate
that year. This lack of action for 1976 contributed to the very depressed cattle market, and of course was another contribution to the ongoing cheap food policy.
The third one was on January 23 or 24 of 1977, when the minister announced the details of his feed cattle support policy for last year. In this policy announcement the minister departed from a traditional departmental announcement which followed a prescribed and accepted pattern or guideline. He changed the rules in two ways: by using 95 per cent of the previous five year average market price instead of 90 per cent, and by using a flat dollar figure of $1.79 to be added to the stabilized level of $40.16 in order to make a payout possible. This $1.79 was the cost of production increment when the feed grains and feeder cattle, the two principal input costs in producing feeder cattle, were both down in 1976. This cost factor should have been a reducing factor.
These are facts and items of debate which should have been brought out in a parliamentary forum at least six months ago, and not now in a politically charged atmosphere. That is the trouble in our Canadian cattle industry-there is far too much politics involved in our market orientation. Why not let the market work?

speakeroldname: Mr. Irenee Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROPOSED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF POLICY STATEMENTS ON CATTLE INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that in asking his question on February 4, 1977, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) acknowledged the importance of the programs which this government has put into place for the benefit of the Canadian cattle industry. The three programs which he mentioned-the cow-calf stabilization program, the slaughter cattle stabilization program, and the beef import quotas-have since been supplemented by an additional program at the request of producers in western Canada. I am speaking, of course, of the drought program.
As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) explained in his response on February 4, he has no objection in principle to the referral of these programs to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for discussion. In fact he would welcome such an opportunity further to explain their value to Canadian cattlemen. However, he is also aware that there is generally a very heavy demand on the time and resources available to both members of committees and the committees' branch itself.
The agriculture committee has recently expended a considerable amount of time and effort in studying the report of the commission of inquiry into the marketing of beef and veal. Issues of concern to the industry, such as those mentioned previously, were provided with an excellent forum for discussion during these meetings. The other place has also been most active in this respect. In addition, the Standing Committee on Agriculture considers the agriculture stabilization estimates, as well as those of the department, each year. Discussions are very broad in scope at these meetings, and issues such as the hon. member has mentioned tonight are regularly discussed with the witnesses who are present.
Although I am aware of the hon. member's concerns as they relate to the cattle industry, I have also noted the specific

July 18, 1977
Adjournment Debate
concerns of other members relative to different commodities. I am sure that the request of the hon. member would, therefore, give rise to a request for discussion by several other commodity interests. In view of the foregoing, and under the present circumstances, I do not believe that the minister would support the hon. member's request.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN FEDERAL SHARE OF COST OF HIGHWAY PROGRAM FOR ATLANTIC REGION
TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN FEDERAL SHARE OF COST OF HIGHWAY PROGRAM FOR ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am debating tonight the reply given me by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in which he advised that he was not prepared to accede to the request by the Atlantic provinces highways ministers and myself for a more deserving cost sharing formula in regard to the $100 million highway strengthening program for the Atlantic region announced recently, other than that the federal government would contribute 50 per cent of the cost.
I say with all due respect to the minister that I find it difficult to reconcile his creating a new precedent when another precedent has been set in two other areas of highway programs. Under the original agreement to build the Trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland during the Pearson regime, the federal government participated to the extent of 90 per cent of the cost. The minister replied to me that he was not sure that the generous treatment offered at that time should necessarily be repeated.
I remind the minister through his parliamentary secretary that even though the portion of the highway through Newfoundland was called the Trans-Canada highway, any similarity between what exists under that name in my province and that which exists in other parts of Canada is strictly coincidental and primarily a misnomer of the worst degree. I feel that on this basis alone the federal government should even pay 100 per cent of the cost to correct the accepted ridiculous standards of that highway in Canada.
Secondly, his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), has entered into several highways agreements with the province of Newfoundland, which are still existing, to build highways in the province on a 90-10 basis.
Thirdly, I wonder at the answers given to me according to which the program for the four Atlantic provinces of $100 million-about $25 million to each province-is deemed to be so generous when a similar amount of almost $100 million is to be provided to one other province under a $264 million Quebec highway program.
I would venture to say that the most deteriorated section of the Trans-Canada highway exists in my province and in my district, the portion from the Port aux Basques entry to Corner-brook, a most important section of the corridor which is so necessary for the highway traffic to St. John's, Newfoundland.
It is interesting to note that in the Quebec agreement the basis of the financial contribution of $100 million is for

industrial development, to facilitate access to tourist areas and, to improve safety and capacity along the traffic corridor, and I can only wonder why it is not recognized that the same need exists for the Newfoundland corridor to give that province the infrastructure base which is so vitally necessary for our economic development and for a fundamental transportation base so that Newfoundland can finally contribute toward the Canadian dream.
Certainly it should be recognized, from the slow progress made in developing and marketing our resources, that a reasonable transportation system is vital in order to overcome the handicap of transportation costs in competing for distant markets where we sell our products.
I hope that the minister will have his officials drive over the Trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland to see the deteriorated sections which are a danger to the traveller, and which can only be termed an embarrassment to Canada. What can our province do with $30 million? Our share of the program can do little to meet the needs, especially when it is spread over a three year period. I can only ask again that the matter be looked into with a view to meeting our regional objectives the fulfillment of which which we have awaited with too much patience over the past years. I hope that the very efficient parliamentary secretary can give me an answer which will give some hope for the future and which will meet the needs of Newfoundland in line with the highways agreement which was signed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN FEDERAL SHARE OF COST OF HIGHWAY PROGRAM FOR ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering the question of an appropriate role for the federal government in supporting the upgrading of the primary highway system in the Atlantic provinces, it is important to recognize that for the most part highways are a provincial responsibility.
However, as evidenced by a recent announcement, the federal government proposes to spend up to $125 million over the next three years to help improve transportation services in the four Atlantic provinces. The major highway strengthening program to which the government will contribute $100 million is, of course, of the highest priority.
An analysis of the highway proposal, or at least of those parts of the proposal that were put forward as having priority in the context of an initial three year agreement, submitted jointly by the provincial governments, indicated that the standardization of minimum truck weight and related regulations would indeed result in significant benefits that could be considered to be national rather than purely provincial in nature. This conclusion formed one of the main arguments in support of federal assistance.
As to the question of the cost-sharing ratio, the government feels that a 50 per cent federal share of the eligible costs would appropriately reflect the extent of "national" interest in the program. And, Mr. Speaker, given the need for fiscal restraint, the federal government is unable to assume additional liability at this time.
July 18, 1977

In conclusion, it is useful, I think, to point out that the federal proposal does make provision for a review of the first three year program, an analysis of future needs, and a recommendation regarding further programming.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-POSITION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS ON PARTICIPATION IN MULTIPARTITE NATIONAL FORUM
LABOUR CONDITIONS-POSITION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS ON PARTICIPATION IN MULTIPARTITE NATIONAL FORUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises out of questions which I asked of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) on July 13 as reported in Hansard commencing on page 7626. On June 13, during a speech which I was making, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) interjected when I was suggesting that the evidence was overwhelming that the Canadian Labour Congress would not take part in the Minister of Labour's multipartite national forum which he has been proposing since last autumn. The Minister of Finance interjected and said, "That's not what they say in private".
Subsequently, on July 13, I asked the Minister of Labour the following question which is reported at page 7626 of Hansard:
Can the minister tell the House whether there have been private talks between the CLC and cabinet ministers which indicate that they are prepared to participate in the multipartite national forum or is the position of the CLC as it has been publicly stated, namely, that they are not prepared to participate in that particular forum?
I do not want to use undue language in this Chamber, but I must advise this House that the minister failed to answer that question because he did not want even to seem to be in disagreement with the Minister of Finance. However, the fact of the matter is that the CLC has never privately, publicly, or in any other way given any support to this multipartite national forum which the minister runs around the country saying is the keystone to labour policy on behalf of the Government of Canada.
I pointed out to the minister the other day that he has no commitments whatsoever from business to support a multipartite national forum. That has been made very clear on a number of occasions, if one refers to the press, but it was made very clear when Mr. Sydney Jackson of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, in a statement which was reported in the Globe and Mail of July 13 of this year, said that the whole idea was just window dressing, that he had not talked to a single leader in industry who agreed to it, and that his understanding was that labour did not support it either.
I put it to the parliamentary secretary, to the Minister of Labour and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and I have put it to the Minister of Finance in the past: how can there be a government policy, and how can ministers go around the country and say seriously that this is the policy, when two of the groups which absolutely must be part of this multipartite national forum-which the Minister of Labour said is to decide the "big economic issues of the day"-labour and management, have not agreed to participate in it? What commitments does the government have from labour? Frankly,
Adjournment Debate
I do not believe there are any. I think the government has been pulling the wool over our eyes for months, and to the degree it is doing that it is destroying the ability of business, labour and the government to get together to have meaningful discussions.
Second, what commitment does the government have from any section of the business community? I do not want to be met tonight with a lot of nonsense about the fact that these are ongoing discussions having something to do with decontrol. When the Minister of Labour put these things forward in October he was not talking about decontrol at all; he was talking about a forum for discussion in the post-control period, not to determine what decontrol is. The Minister of Finance confirmed to me some days ago in the House that his discussions which are going on right now are not in the multipartite sense but are strictly with business and labour.
I think it is time the Minister of Labour and the government generally stopped this silly little dance of pretending to have policy when they do not have it, and they do not have the support of the sectors of the community-meaning labour and business-which they must have to support the proposal which was put forward by the Minister of Labour. It would be far better to admit that, and come up with another idea. It is absolute folly to continue to waste public funds by putting out public documentation, advertising brochures and the like, which have been appearing on all hon. members' desks recently touting a multipartite national forum to decide the big economic issues of the day many months after it was first proposed when in fact there is no agreement from either labour or business to participate in it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Irenee Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-POSITION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS ON PARTICIPATION IN MULTIPARTITE NATIONAL FORUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the recent report of the executive director of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association presented at its annual general meeting, the following statement appears:
... the Association has not fully assessed all of the 14 initiatives proposed by the federal Minister of Labour for improving labour relation climate ...
This makes it all the more difficult to be able to conclude that the statement of any representative of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association does, in fact, represent the considered views of that association on the basis of an appropriately careful evaluation of any of the 14 points, including the national consultative forum.
Over the past number of months the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the officials of his department have gone to considerable lengths to consult with business and labour across this country with regard to the 14-point program. They have heard the concerns of businessmen for such issues as the competitiveness of Canadian industry in international markets, productivity, wages, and the climate of industrial relations within which economic decisions will have to be made once controls will have been lifted. They have also heard new and much more broadly framed concerns of organized labour for a more influential voice in matters of broad social and economic consequence. The very consultations in which we have engaged
7774

July 18, 1977
Adjournment Debate
regarding the 14 points have already served to broaden the perspectives from which labour, business, and government look at matters of common interest and concern.
This process of enlarging the awareness of the other person's interests and points of view can be a powerful force for bringing greater wisdom into economic decisions, especially if the various considerations are brought into focus for intelligent analysis and consideration by all interested groups and individuals through the mechanism of the proposed national consultative forum. The forum we envisage would be representative not only of business, labour and government, but also of other interest areas including, but not necessarily restricted to, consumers, co-operatives, professionals, and primary producers such as farmers and fishermen.
Our assessment of the numerous consultations we have had with business and labour about the forum is that the concept
has been enthusiastically endorsed and generally enjoys a wide measure of support. Indeed we have found no one who is actually opposed to consultation among those concerned with and affected by decisions on economic and social matters. The report of the executive director of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association referred to above contains references to consultations in which the association has been involved, and the contexts of those references would lead one to conclude that the C.M.A. has just as much to gain from consultation as anyone else.
